title: Book 5, Chapter 16 — Feeling against Sparta in Peloponnese—League of the Mantineans, Eleans, Argives, and Athenians—Battle of Mantinea and breaking up of the League
paragraphs: The treaty and alliance between the Lacedaemonians and Athenians were concluded after the ten years’ war, in the ephorate of Pleistolas at Lacedaemon and the archonship of Alcaeus at Athens. The states that had accepted them were at peace. But the Corinthians and some of the cities in Peloponnese tried to disturb the settlement, and the allies at once began a fresh agitation against Lacedaemon. As time went on, the Athenians also came to suspect the Lacedaemonians, because they did not carry out some of the provisions of the treaty. For six years and ten months the two powers kept from invading each other’s territory. Abroad, however, the unstable armistice did not stop either of them from doing the other the most effective harm it could, until at last they were forced to break the treaty made after the ten years’ war and return to open hostilities.

The same Thucydides, an Athenian, has also written the history of this period, in the order of events by summers and winters, down to the time when the Lacedaemonians and their allies put an end to the Athenian empire and took the Long Walls and Piraeus. By then the war had lasted twenty-seven years in all. Only a mistaken judgment can object to counting the interval of treaty as part of the war. Look at it in the light of the facts and it cannot reasonably be considered a state of peace. Neither side either gave or got back all that it had agreed to. Besides, there were violations on both sides in the Mantinean and Epidaurian wars and other cases, the allies in the direction of Thrace were as openly hostile as ever, and the Boeotians had only a truce renewed every ten days. So the first ten years’ war, the treacherous armistice that followed it, and the war after that, if we reckon by the seasons, make up the number of years I have mentioned, give or take a few days. They also provide a case in which faith in oracles was for once justified by the event. I certainly remember that from the beginning to the end of the war it was commonly said that it would last thrice nine years. I lived through the whole of it, old enough to understand events, and I paid attention to them in order to learn the exact truth about them. It was also my fate to be an exile from my country for twenty years after my command at Amphipolis. Being present with both parties, and especially with the Peloponnesians because of my exile, I had leisure to observe affairs rather closely. I will now therefore relate the differences that arose after the ten years’ war, the breach of the treaty, and the hostilities that followed.

After the fifty years’ truce and the alliance that followed it were concluded, the embassies from Peloponnese that had been summoned for this business returned from Lacedaemon. The rest went straight home, but the Corinthians first turned aside to Argos and opened negotiations with some of the men in office there. They pointed out that Lacedaemon could have no good end in view, only the subjugation of Peloponnese, or she would never have entered into treaty and alliance with the once detested Athenians. The duty of consulting for the safety of Peloponnese had now fallen upon Argos. Argos should immediately pass a decree inviting any Hellenic state that chose — provided it was independent and accustomed to meet fellow powers on the fair and equal ground of law and justice — to make a defensive alliance with the Argives. She should appoint a few individuals with full powers to negotiate, instead of making the people the medium of negotiation, so that if an applicant were rejected, the fact of his overture would not become public. They said that many would come over out of hatred of the Lacedaemonians. After explaining their views in this way, the Corinthians returned home.

Those with whom they had spoken carried the proposal to their government and people. The Argives passed the decree and chose twelve men to negotiate an alliance with any Hellenic state that wished one. Athens and Lacedaemon alone were excluded: neither could be admitted without a reference to the Argive people. Argos adopted the plan the more readily for two reasons. She saw that war with Lacedaemon was inevitable, because the truce was close to expiring, and she hoped to win the supremacy of Peloponnese. Lacedaemon’s disasters had by now lowered her very far in public estimation, whereas the Argives were thriving. They had taken no part in the Attic war, and their neutrality had on the contrary brought them large profits. So the Argives made ready to receive into alliance any Hellenes who wanted it.

The Mantineans and their allies were the first to come over, out of fear of the Lacedaemonians. They had used the war against Athens to bring a large part of Arcadia into subjection. Now that Lacedaemon had leisure to interfere, they thought she would not leave them undisturbed in their conquests, and so they gladly turned to a powerful city like Argos, the historical enemy of the Lacedaemonians and a sister democracy. When Mantinea defected, the rest of Peloponnese at once began to debate whether to follow her example, reasoning that the Mantineans would not have changed sides without good cause. They were also angry with Lacedaemon, among other reasons, for having inserted in the treaty with Athens that it should be consistent with their oaths for both parties, Lacedaemonians and Athenians, to add to it or take away from it at their discretion. This clause was the real origin of the panic in Peloponnese, since it aroused suspicions of a combination between Lacedaemonians and Athenians against their liberties. Any alteration should properly have been made conditional on the consent of the whole body of the allies. With these apprehensions, there was a very general desire in each state to place itself in alliance with Argos.

Meanwhile the Lacedaemonians perceived the agitation in Peloponnese. They saw that Corinth had started it and was herself on the point of allying with the Argives, and they sent ambassadors to Corinth in the hope of stopping what was planned. They charged her with causing it all. If she deserted Lacedaemon and became the ally of Argos, they said, she would add the breaking of her oaths to the crime she had already committed by refusing the treaty with Athens, for it had been expressly agreed that the majority of the allies should decide, unless the gods or heroes stood in the way. Corinth answered in the presence of those allies who, like her, had refused the treaty and whom she had invited beforehand to attend. She did not openly state the wrongs she complained of, such as the failure to get Sollium or Anactorium back from the Athenians, or any other point on which she felt she had been injured. She sheltered instead behind the pretext that she could not abandon her Thracian allies. She had given them her own separate pledge of security when they first rebelled together with Potidæa, and on later occasions as well. She therefore denied breaking her oaths to the allies by staying out of the treaty with Athens. She had sworn by the gods to her Thracian friends, and she could not honestly betray them. Besides, the wording was, “unless the gods or heroes stand in the way.” And here, as it seemed to her, the gods did stand in the way. So much for her earlier oaths. On the Argive alliance, she would consult her friends and do whatever was right. The Lacedaemonian envoys went home. Some Argive ambassadors, who happened to be in Corinth, then urged her to conclude the alliance without further delay, but were told to come to the next congress, which was to be held at Corinth.

Immediately afterwards an Elean embassy arrived. They first made an alliance with Corinth and then, as instructed, went on to Argos and became allies of the Argives, since their country was just then at enmity with Lacedaemon and Lepreum. Some time before, there had been a war between the Lepreans and some of the Arcadians. The Eleans, called in by the Lepreans with the offer of half their lands, had put an end to the war. They left the land in the hands of its Leprean occupiers and imposed on them a tribute of a talent to the Olympian Zeus. Until the Attic war the Lepreans paid this tribute. Then they took the war as an excuse to stop paying, and when the Eleans used force they appealed to Lacedaemon. The case was thus submitted to her arbitration, but the Eleans suspected the fairness of the tribunal, withdrew from the reference and laid waste the Leprean territory. The Lacedaemonians nevertheless decided that the Lepreans were independent and the Eleans the aggressors, and when the latter would not abide by the arbitration, they sent a garrison of heavy infantry into Lepreum. Thereupon the Eleans, holding that Lacedaemon had taken in one of their rebel subjects, put forward the convention providing that each ally should come out of the Attic war in possession of what he had when he went into it. Considering that justice had not been done them, they went over to the Argives, and now made the alliance through their ambassadors, who had been instructed for that purpose. Immediately after them the Corinthians and the Thracian Chalcidians became allies of Argos. Meanwhile the Boeotians and Megarians, who acted together, remained quiet. Lacedaemon left them to do as they pleased, and they thought that the Argive democracy would not suit their aristocratic government as well as the Lacedaemonian constitution did.

About this time in the same summer, Athens succeeded in reducing Scione. She killed the adult males, enslaved the women and children, and gave the land to the Plataeans to live on. She also restored the Delians to Delos, moved both by her reverses in the field and by the commands of the god at Delphi. Meanwhile the Phocians and Locrians went to war with each other. The Corinthians and Argives, now allied, went to Tegea to detach it from Lacedaemon. They reasoned that if so considerable a state could be won over, all Peloponnese would be with them. But the Tegeans declared that they would do nothing against Lacedaemon. The Corinthians, until then eager, slackened their efforts and began to fear that none of the rest would now come over. Still, they went to the Boeotians and tried to persuade them to an alliance with Argos and themselves, and to common action generally. They also begged them to accompany them to Athens and win for them a ten days’ truce like the one made between the Athenians and Boeotians not long after the fifty years’ treaty. If the Athenians refused, the Boeotians were to throw up the armistice and make no truce in future without Corinth. These were the requests of the Corinthians. The Boeotians would not hear of the Argive alliance, but went with them to Athens. There they failed to get the ten days’ truce, for the Athenians answered that the Corinthians already had a truce, being allies of Lacedaemon. The Boeotians nevertheless kept their ten days’ truce, in spite of the Corinthians’ prayers and their reproaches for the breach of faith. The Corinthians had to make do with a de facto armistice with Athens.

The same summer the Lacedaemonians marched into Arcadia with their whole levy, under Pleistoanax, son of Pausanias, king of Lacedaemon. Their target was the Parrhasians, subjects of Mantinea, a faction of whom had called for their help. They also intended, if they could, to tear down the fort of Cypsela, which the Mantineans had built and manned in Parrhasian territory to harass the district of Sciritis in Laconia. The Lacedaemonians ravaged the Parrhasian country. The Mantineans handed their town over to an Argive garrison and turned to the defense of their confederacy, but they were unable to save Cypsela or the Parrhasian towns, and went back to Mantinea. Meanwhile the Lacedaemonians made the Parrhasians independent, razed the fortress, and went home.

The same summer the soldiers from Thrace who had gone out with Brasidas came back; Clearidas had brought them from there after the treaty. The Lacedaemonians decreed that the Helots who had fought with Brasidas should be free and allowed to live where they liked. Not long afterwards they settled them with the Neodamodes at Lepreum, which lies on the Laconian and Elean border, Lacedaemon being at this time at enmity with Elis. As for those Spartans who had been taken prisoner on the island and had surrendered their arms, it was feared that they might suppose they were to be subjected to some degradation because of their misfortune, and so attempt a revolution if left in possession of their franchise. They were therefore at once disfranchised, although some of them were in office at the time. This put them under a disability to hold office or to buy and sell anything. After some time, however, the franchise was restored to them.

The same summer the Dians took Thyssus, a town on Acte by Athos, in alliance with Athens. Throughout the summer the Athenians and Peloponnesians kept up their dealings with each other, although each side began to suspect the other directly after the treaty, because the places named in it had not been given back. The duty of beginning the restoration of Amphipolis and the other towns had fallen to Lacedaemon, and she had not done it. She had also failed to get the treaty accepted by her Thracian allies, the Boeotians and the Corinthians, though she kept promising to join Athens in forcing them to comply if they went on refusing. She kept fixing a date after which those still refusing to enter would be declared enemies of both parties, but she took care not to bind herself to this in writing. The Athenians, for their part, saw none of these professions turned into fact, and began to doubt the honesty of her intentions. So they not only rejected her demands for Pylos, but regretted having given up the prisoners from the island, and held on tight to the other places until Lacedaemon should fulfill her part of the treaty. Lacedaemon replied that she had done what she could. She had given up the Athenian prisoners of war she held, withdrawn from Thrace, and done everything else within her power. Amphipolis she was unable to restore, but she would try to bring the Boeotians and Corinthians into the treaty, to recover Panactum, and to send home all the Athenian prisoners of war in Boeotia. Meanwhile she demanded that Pylos be given back, or at any rate that the Messenians and Helots be removed, just as her own troops had been removed from Thrace, and that the place be garrisoned, if need be, by the Athenians themselves. After a number of conferences during the summer, she persuaded Athens to take the Messenians and the other Helots and deserters from Laconia out of Pylos. Athens settled them at Cranii in Cephallenia. So throughout this summer there was peace and dealing between the two peoples.

In the next winter, however, the ephors who had made the treaty were out of office, and some of their successors were flatly opposed to it. Embassies now came from the Lacedaemonian confederacy, and the Athenians, Boeotians and Corinthians also appeared at Lacedaemon. After much discussion they reached no agreement and left for their several homes. Cleobulus and Xenares, the two ephors most eager to break off the treaty, used the occasion to speak privately with the Boeotians and Corinthians. They urged them to act together as far as possible. They told the Boeotians first to ally themselves with Argos, and then to try to bring both themselves and the Argives into alliance with Lacedaemon. That way the Boeotians would be least likely to be forced into the Attic treaty, and the Lacedaemonians would rather win the friendship and alliance of Argos, even at the price of Athenian hostility and a broken treaty. The Boeotians knew that Lacedaemon had long desired an honorable friendship with Argos, since the Lacedaemonians believed it would make the conduct of the war outside Peloponnese considerably easier. At the same time they begged the Boeotians to put Panactum into her hands, so that she might, if possible, get Pylos in exchange for it, and so be better placed to resume hostilities with Athens.

Once they had received these instructions for their governments from Xenares, Cleobulus and their friends at Lacedaemon, the Boeotians and Corinthians left. On the road home, two high officials of Argos, who had waited for them there, joined them. These sounded them out on whether the Boeotians might join the Corinthians, Eleans and Mantineans in allying with Argos. Their idea was that, once united, they could make peace or war as they chose, against Lacedaemon or any other power. The Boeotian envoys were pleased to be asked by chance to do the very thing their friends at Lacedaemon had told them to do. The two Argives saw that their proposal was welcome and went away, promising to send ambassadors to the Boeotians. When the Boeotians reached home, they reported to the Boeotarchs what had been said to them at Lacedaemon and by the Argives they had met. The Boeotarchs were pleased with the idea and took it up with all the more eagerness because of the lucky coincidence that Argos was asking for the very thing their friends at Lacedaemon wanted. Soon afterwards ambassadors came from Argos with the proposals described. The Boeotarchs approved the terms and sent the ambassadors away with a promise to send envoys to Argos to negotiate the alliance.

In the meantime the Boeotarchs, the Corinthians, the Megarians and the envoys from Thrace decided first to exchange oaths with each other, to give help to each other whenever it was required and to make neither war nor peace except in common. After that the Boeotians and Megarians, who acted together, were to make the alliance with Argos. But before the oaths were taken, the Boeotarchs communicated these proposals to the four councils of the Boeotians, in whom the supreme power resides. They advised them to exchange oaths with all such cities as were willing to enter into a defensive league with the Boeotians. But the members of the Boeotian councils refused their assent, afraid of offending Lacedaemon by entering into a league with the deserter Corinth. The Boeotarchs had not told them what had passed at Lacedaemon, or about the advice given by Cleobulus and Xenares and the Boeotian partisans there, namely that they should become allies of Corinth and Argos as a preliminary to a junction with Lacedaemon. They had fancied that, even if they said nothing about this, the councils would not vote against what the Boeotarchs had decided and advised. When this difficulty arose, the Corinthians and the envoys from Thrace departed without anything having been concluded. The Boeotarchs had previously intended, after carrying this, to try to effect the alliance with Argos. Now they omitted to bring the Argive question before the councils, and did not send to Argos the envoys they had promised. A general coldness and delay ensued in the matter.
In this same winter the Olynthians assaulted and took Mecyberna, which had an Athenian garrison inside it.

All this time negotiations had continued between the Athenians and Lacedaemonians over the conquests each still held. Lacedaemon hoped that if Athens recovered Panactum from the Boeotians, she herself might recover Pylos. She now sent an embassy to the Boeotians, begging them to put Panactum and their Athenian prisoners into her hands, so that she could exchange them for Pylos. The Boeotians refused unless Lacedaemon made a separate alliance with them, as she had with Athens. Lacedaemon knew this would be a breach of faith toward Athens, since both had agreed that neither would make peace or war without the other. But she wanted Panactum, which she hoped to exchange for Pylos, and the party urging the dissolution of the treaty was strongly in favor of the Boeotian connection. So she finally concluded the alliance just as winter was turning to spring, and Panactum was razed at once. And so the eleventh year of the war ended.

In the first days of the following summer, the Argives noticed that the promised ambassadors from Boeotia had not come, that Panactum was being demolished, and that the Boeotians and Lacedaemonians had concluded a separate alliance. They grew afraid that Argos would be left alone while the entire confederacy went over to Lacedaemon. They imagined that the Lacedaemonians had persuaded the Boeotians to raze Panactum and to enter the treaty with the Athenians, and that Athens knew of this arrangement. Thus even the Athenian alliance, a resource on which they had always counted because of the existing dissensions, in case their treaty with Lacedaemon lapsed, was no longer open to them. In this strait the Argives feared that, having refused to renew the treaty with Lacedaemon and aspired to the supremacy in Peloponnese, they would find the Lacedaemonians, Tegeans, Boeotians and Athenians all on their hands at once. They therefore hastily sent Eustrophus and Aeson, who seemed the men most likely to be welcome, as envoys to Lacedaemon. Their aim was to make as good a treaty as they could, on whatever terms were obtainable, and to be left in peace.

When their ambassadors reached Lacedaemon, they set about negotiating the terms of the proposed treaty. The Argives began by demanding the right to submit to the arbitration of some state or private person the question of the Cynurian land. This is a frontier territory that they have always disputed. It contains the towns of Thyrea and Anthene, and the Lacedaemonians occupy it. The Lacedaemonians first replied that this point could not even be discussed, and that they were ready to conclude on the old terms. In the end, however, the Argive ambassadors won from them this concession. For the present there would be a truce of fifty years. But either party would be free, so long as neither plague nor war was afflicting Lacedaemon or Argos, to issue a formal challenge and settle the question of this territory by battle, as had been done once before when both sides claimed the victory. Pursuit would not be permitted beyond the frontier of Argos or Lacedaemon. The Lacedaemonians at first thought this sheer folly. At last, however, being anxious at any price to have the friendship of Argos, they agreed to the terms demanded and had them written down. Before any of this took effect, though, the ambassadors were to go back to Argos and consult their people, and, if the people approved, to come at the feast of the Hyacinthia and swear the oaths.

The envoys went back accordingly. Meanwhile, as the Argives were occupied with these negotiations, the Lacedaemonian ambassadors Andromedes, Phaedimus and Antimenidas had gone to take the prisoners from the Boeotians and restore both them and Panactum to the Athenians. They found that the Boeotians had already razed Panactum themselves. Their excuse was that their people and the Athenians had long ago exchanged oaths, after a dispute over the place, that neither would live there and that both would graze it in common. The Athenian prisoners of war held by the Boeotians were handed over to Andromedes and his colleagues, who brought them to Athens and returned them. At the same time the envoys announced that Panactum had been razed, which seemed to them as good as restoring it, since it would no longer shelter an enemy of Athens. The Athenians heard this with great indignation. They felt that the Lacedaemonians had deceived them, first in demolishing Panactum, which should have been returned to them standing, and then in making, as they now learned, a separate alliance with the Boeotians, despite their earlier promise to join Athens in compelling those who refused the treaty to accept it. The Athenians also took account of the other points on which Lacedaemon had failed to keep her agreement. Thinking themselves cheated, they gave the ambassadors an angry answer and sent them away.

Now that the quarrel between the Lacedaemonians and Athenians had gone so far, the party at Athens that wanted to cancel the treaty promptly went into action. Foremost among them was Alcibiades, son of Clinias, who was still a young man for any other Hellenic city but was distinguished by the splendor of his ancestry. Alcibiades really thought the Argive alliance preferable, though wounded pride had also a great deal to do with his opposition. The Lacedaemonians had negotiated the treaty through Nicias and Laches and passed him over because of his youth, and he resented this. He resented too that they had not honored the ancient connection between his family and them as their proxeni. His grandfather had renounced it, and he had himself lately thought of renewing it by attentions to their prisoners taken on the island. Slighted, as he thought, on every side, he had at first spoken against the treaty, saying that the Lacedaemonians could not be trusted and were treating only so as to crush Argos by this means and afterwards attack Athens alone. Now, immediately after the events above, he sent a private message to the Argives, telling them to come to Athens as quickly as possible, with the Mantineans and Eleans, and propose an alliance. The moment was favorable, he said, and he would do all he could to help them.

When this message reached them, the Argives learned that the Athenians, far from sharing in the Boeotian alliance, were in a serious quarrel with the Lacedaemonians. They stopped caring about the embassy they had just sent to Lacedaemon on the treaty, and began to lean toward the Athenians instead. They reflected that, if war came, they would have on their side a city that was an ancient ally of Argos, a sister democracy and very strong at sea. So they immediately sent ambassadors to Athens to treat for an alliance, accompanied by others from Elis and Mantinea.

At the same time an embassy hurried from Lacedaemon, made up of men thought to be friendly to the Athenians: Philocharidas, Leon and Endius. They feared that the Athenians, in their irritation, might ally themselves with the Argives. They also came to ask for Pylos in exchange for Panactum, and to argue, in defense of the Boeotian alliance, that it had not been made to harm the Athenians. The envoys made these points in the senate and said that they had come with full powers to settle all the other questions between the two cities. Alcibiades grew afraid that if they repeated this to the popular assembly, they might win over the multitude and the Argive alliance might be rejected. So he resorted to a stratagem. By a solemn assurance he persuaded the Lacedaemonians that if they said nothing in the assembly about their full powers, he would give them Pylos back (he, its present opponent, undertaking to obtain this from the Athenians) and would settle the other points at issue. His plan was to separate them from Nicias, to discredit them before the people as insincere in their intentions or even inconsistent in what they said, and so to have the Argives, Eleans and Mantineans taken into alliance. The plan worked. The envoys appeared before the people and were asked the question, and they did not say, as they had said in the senate, that they had come with full powers. The Athenians lost all patience. Carried away by Alcibiades, who thundered louder than ever against the Lacedaemonians, they were ready at once to bring in the Argives and their companions and take them into alliance. But an earthquake occurred before anything definite was done, and the assembly was adjourned.

At the assembly held the next day, Nicias still maintained that it was best to remain friends with the Lacedaemonians. They had been deceived themselves, and had let him be deceived too, by not admitting that they had come with full powers. Even so, he held that the Argive proposals should be left standing, and that the Athenians should send once more to Lacedaemon to learn her intentions. Postponing the war could only add to the prestige of Athens and damage that of her rivals. Athenian affairs were in excellent condition, so it was in their interest to preserve this prosperity as long as possible, while those of Lacedaemon were so desperate that the sooner she could try her fortune again the better. He persuaded them, accordingly, to send ambassadors, himself among them. They were to invite the Lacedaemonians, if they were really sincere, to restore Panactum intact together with Amphipolis, and to abandon their alliance with the Boeotians unless the Boeotians consented to accede to the treaty. This followed the stipulation that neither party might treat without the other. The ambassadors were also to say that the Athenians, had they wished to play false, might already have made an alliance with the Argives, who had in fact come to Athens for that very purpose. They left with instructions on any other complaints the Athenians had to make. When they reached Lacedaemon, they delivered their instructions and ended by saying this: unless the Lacedaemonians gave up their alliance with the Boeotians, in the event that the Boeotians would not accede to the treaty, the Athenians for their part would ally themselves with the Argives and their friends. The Lacedaemonians, however, refused to give up the Boeotian alliance. The party of Xenares the ephor, and those who shared his view, carried the day on this point. They did renew the oaths, at the request of Nicias, who feared to return having accomplished nothing and to be disgraced, as indeed was his fate, since he was held to be the author of the treaty with Lacedaemon. When he returned, the Athenians heard that nothing had been done at Lacedaemon. They flew into a passion and decided that faith had not been kept with them. They took advantage of the presence of the Argives and their allies, who had been introduced by Alcibiades, and made a treaty and alliance with them on the following terms:
The Athenians, Argives, Mantineans and Eleans, acting for themselves and for the allies in their respective empires, made a treaty for a hundred years, to be without fraud or harm by land and by sea.

1. It shall not be lawful, by any means whatsoever, for the Argives, Eleans, Mantineans and their allies to carry on war against the Athenians or the allies in the Athenian empire, or for the Athenians and their allies to carry on war against the Argives, Eleans, Mantineans or their allies.
The Athenians, Argives, Eleans and Mantineans shall be allies for a hundred years on the following terms:

2. If an enemy invades the country of the Athenians, the Argives, Eleans and Mantineans shall go to the relief of Athens, as the Athenians may require by message, in whatever way they most effectively can, to the best of their power. But if the invader has gone away after plundering the territory, the offending state shall be the enemy of the Argives, Mantineans, Eleans and Athenians, and all these cities shall make war against it. None of the cities shall be able to make peace with that state unless all the above cities agree to do so.

3. Likewise the Athenians shall go to the relief of Argos, Mantinea and Elis, if an enemy invades the country of Elis, Mantinea or Argos, as the above cities may require by message, in whatever way they most effectively can, to the best of their power. But if the invader has gone away after plundering the territory, the offending state shall be the enemy of the Athenians, Argives, Mantineans and Eleans, and all these cities shall make war against it. Peace may not be made with that state unless all the above cities agree to it.

4. No armed force shall be allowed to pass for hostile purposes through the country of the contracting powers, or of the allies in their respective empires, or to go by sea, unless all the cities — that is to say, Athens, Argos, Mantinea and Elis — vote for such passage.

5. The relieving troops shall be maintained by the city sending them for thirty days from their arrival in the city that has requested them, and in the same way upon their return. If their services are wanted for a longer period, the city that sent for them shall maintain them, at the rate of three Aeginetan obols per day for a heavy-armed soldier, archer or light soldier, and an Aeginetan drachma for a trooper.

6. The city sending for the troops shall have the command when the war is in its own country. But if the cities resolve upon a joint expedition, the command shall be divided equally among all the cities.

7. The treaty shall be sworn to by the Athenians for themselves and their allies, and by the Argives, Mantineans, Eleans and their allies, each state individually. Each shall swear the oath most binding in its own country, over full-grown victims. The oath shall be as follows:
“I STAND BY THE ALLIANCE AND ITS ARTICLES, JUSTLY, INNOCENTLY AND SINCERELY, AND I WILL NOT TRANSGRESS THEM IN ANY WAY OR BY ANY MEANS WHATSOEVER.”

The oath shall be taken at Athens by the Senate and the magistrates, and the Prytanes shall administer it. At Argos, the Senate, the Eighty and the Artynae take it, and the Eighty administer it. At Mantinea, the Demiurgi, the Senate and the other magistrates take it, and the Theori and Polemarchs administer it. At Elis, the Demiurgi, the magistrates and the Six Hundred take it, and the Demiurgi and the Thesmophylaces administer it. The oaths are to be renewed thirty days before the Olympic games, when the Athenians go to Elis, Mantinea and Argos, and ten days before the great feast of the Panathenaea, when the Argives, Mantineans and Eleans go to Athens. The articles of the treaty, the oaths and the alliance are to be inscribed on a stone pillar: by the Athenians in the citadel, by the Argives in the market-place, in the temple of Apollo, and by the Mantineans in the temple of Zeus, in the market-place. The cities are also to erect a brazen pillar jointly at the Olympic games now at hand. If the above cities see good to add anything to these articles, whatever all of them agree upon after consulting together shall be binding.

The treaty and alliances were thus concluded, but neither the Lacedaemonians nor the Athenians renounced the treaty between them. Meanwhile Corinth, although the ally of the Argives, did not accede to the new treaty. She had likewise held back from the earlier alliance, defensive and offensive, formed between the Eleans, Argives and Mantineans. On that occasion she had declared herself content with the first alliance, which was defensive only and bound the members to help each other, but not to join in attacking anyone. The Corinthians thus stood aloof from their allies and again turned their thoughts toward Lacedaemon.

At the Olympic games held this summer, in which the Arcadian Androsthenes was victor for the first time in the wrestling and boxing, the Eleans excluded the Lacedaemonians from the temple. They were thus prevented from sacrificing or competing, because they had refused to pay the fine the Eleans imposed on them under the Olympic law. The Eleans alleged that the Lacedaemonians had attacked Fort Phyrcus and sent heavy infantry of theirs into Lepreum during the Olympic truce. The fine was two thousand minae, two for each heavy-armed soldier, as the law prescribes. The Lacedaemonians sent envoys and pleaded that the imposition was unjust. They said that the truce had not yet been proclaimed at Lacedaemon when the heavy infantry were sent off. But the Eleans affirmed that the armistice with them had already begun (they proclaim it first among themselves), and that the aggression of the Lacedaemonians had taken them by surprise, living quietly as in time of peace and expecting nothing. The Lacedaemonians answered that if the Eleans really believed they had committed an aggression, it was useless after that to proclaim the truce at Lacedaemon. They had proclaimed it all the same, because they believed nothing of the kind, and from that moment the Lacedaemonians had made no attack upon the Elean country. Nevertheless the Eleans held to what they had said: nothing would persuade them that an aggression had not been committed. If, however, the Lacedaemonians would restore Lepreum, they would give up their own share of the money and pay the god’s share for them.

This proposal was not accepted, so the Eleans tried a second. If the Lacedaemonians objected to restoring Lepreum, they should instead ascend the altar of the Olympian Zeus, since they were so anxious to have access to the temple, and swear before the Hellenes that they would surely pay the fine at a later day. This was also refused, and the Lacedaemonians were excluded from the temple, the sacrifice and the games, and sacrificed at home. The Lepreans were the only other Hellenes who did not attend. Still, the Eleans were afraid that the Lacedaemonians would sacrifice by force, and kept guard with a heavy-armed company of their young men. A thousand Argives and the same number of Mantineans joined them, along with some Athenian cavalry who stayed at Harpina during the feast. Great fears were felt in the assembly that the Lacedaemonians would come in arms, especially after Lichas, son of Arcesilaus, a Lacedaemonian, had been scourged on the course by the umpires. His horses had won, but the Boeotian people were proclaimed the victor, because he had no right to enter. So he came forward on the course and crowned the charioteer, to show that the chariot was his. After this incident all were more afraid than ever and firmly expected a disturbance. The Lacedaemonians, however, kept quiet and let the feast pass by, as we have seen. After the Olympic games, the Argives and the allies went to Corinth to invite her to come over to them. They found some Lacedaemonian envoys there, and a long discussion followed, which ended in nothing, since an earthquake occurred and they dispersed to their different homes.

Summer was now over. In the following winter the Heracleots in Trachinia fought a battle against the Aenianians, Dolopians, Malians and some of the Thessalians. All these tribes bordered on the town and were hostile to it, because it directly menaced their country. They had opposed and harassed it from its very foundation by every means they had, and in this battle they defeated the Heracleots. Among the slain was Xenares, son of Cnidis, their Lacedaemonian commander. So the winter ended, and the twelfth year of this war with it. Heraclea was left so badly reduced by the battle that in the first days of the summer following, the Boeotians took over the place. They sent away the Lacedaemonian Agesippidas for misgovernment, since they feared that the Athenians might take the town while the Lacedaemonians were distracted with the affairs of Peloponnese. The Lacedaemonians, nevertheless, were offended at what they had done.

The same summer Alcibiades, son of Clinias, who was now one of the generals at Athens, went into Peloponnese in concert with the Argives and the allies. He took a few Athenian heavy infantry and archers, and picked up some of the allies in those parts as he passed. With this army he marched here and there through Peloponnese and settled various matters connected with the alliance. Among other things, he induced the Patrians to carry their walls down to the sea, and he planned to build a fort himself near the Achaean Rhium. But the Corinthians and Sicyonians, and all the others who would have suffered from a fort there, came up and put a stop to it.

The same summer the Epidaurians and Argives went to war. The pretext was an offering for pasture-land that the Epidaurians owed to Apollo Pythaeus and had not sent, although they were bound to; the Argives had the chief management of the temple. Apart from this pretext, however, Alcibiades and the Argives were determined to gain possession of Epidaurus if they could. That would secure the neutrality of Corinth, and it would give the Athenians a shorter route for reinforcements from Aegina than sailing round Scyllaeum. So the Argives prepared to invade Epidaurus alone and exact the offering.

About the same time the Lacedaemonians marched out with all their people to Leuctra on their frontier, opposite Mount Lycaeum, under Agis, son of Archidamus. Nobody knew where they were going, not even the cities that sent the contingents. But the sacrifices for crossing the frontier were not favorable, so the Lacedaemonians returned home. They told the allies to be ready to march after the next month, which happened to be Carneus, a holy time for the Dorians. Once the Lacedaemonians had withdrawn, the Argives marched out on the last day but three of the month before Carneus. They kept that date throughout their whole time in the field, and invaded and plundered Epidaurus. The Epidaurians called on their allies for help. Some of these gave the month as an excuse; others came as far as the frontier of Epidaurus and stayed there doing nothing.

While the Argives were in Epidaurus, embassies from the cities assembled at Mantinea, at the invitation of the Athenians. When the conference began, the Corinthian Euphamidas said that their actions did not agree with their words. While they sat deliberating about peace, the Epidaurians and their allies and the Argives stood arrayed against each other in arms. Deputies from each party should first go and separate the armies, and then the talk about peace could be resumed. They accepted this suggestion, went and brought the Argives back from Epidaurus, and afterwards reassembled. But they came no nearer to a conclusion, and the Argives invaded Epidaurus a second time and plundered the country. The Lacedaemonians also marched out to Caryae, but the frontier sacrifices again proved unfavorable, and they went back. The Argives ravaged about a third of the Epidaurian territory and then returned home. Meanwhile a thousand Athenian heavy infantry had come to their aid under the command of Alcibiades. They found that the Lacedaemonian expedition was at an end and that they were no longer wanted, and went back again.

So the summer passed. The following winter the Lacedaemonians slipped past the watch of the Athenians and sent three hundred men into Epidaurus as a garrison, under Agesippidas. The Argives then went to the Athenians and complained that they had let an enemy pass by sea, although the treaty had a clause forbidding the allies to let an enemy through their country. They said that unless the Athenians now settled the Messenians and Helots at Pylos to harass the Lacedaemonians, they, the Argives, would consider that faith had not been kept with them. Alcibiades persuaded the Athenians to write at the foot of the Laconian pillar that the Lacedaemonians had not kept their oaths, and to move the Helots at Cranii to Pylos to plunder the country. In other respects they stayed quiet as before. During this winter the Argives and Epidaurians kept up hostilities, with no pitched battle but only forays and ambuscades, in which the losses were small and fell sometimes on one side and sometimes on the other. At the close of the winter, near the beginning of spring, the Argives went to Epidaurus with scaling ladders. They expected the war to have left it unguarded, so that they could take it by assault, but they came back without success. So the winter ended, and with it the thirteenth year of the war.

In the middle of the next summer the Lacedaemonians saw their allies the Epidaurians in distress, and the rest of Peloponnese in revolt or disaffected. They concluded that it was high time to step in if they wanted to check the spread of the evil. They took the field against Argos with their full force, Helots included, under Agis, son of Archidamus, king of the Lacedaemonians. The Tegeans and the other Arcadian allies of Lacedaemon joined the expedition. The allies from the rest of Peloponnese and from beyond it gathered at Phlius. The Boeotians brought five thousand heavy infantry, as many light troops, five hundred horse and the same number of dismounted troopers. The Corinthians brought two thousand heavy infantry, the others brought more or fewer as it happened, and the Phliasians came with all their forces, since the army was in their country.

The Argives had known of the Lacedaemonian preparations from the start, but they took the field only when the enemy was already on the road to join the rest at Phlius. The Mantineans with their allies reinforced them, and so did three thousand Elean heavy infantry. They advanced and met the Lacedaemonians at Methydrium in Arcadia. Each side took a position on a hill, and the Argives prepared to fight the Lacedaemonians while these were still alone. But Agis broke camp in the night and got away, and went on to join the rest of the allies at Phlius. At daybreak the Argives found this out. They marched first to Argos and then to the Nemean road, expecting the Lacedaemonians and their allies to come down that way. Agis, however, did not take the road they expected. He gave his orders to the Lacedaemonians, Arcadians and Epidaurians, took another difficult road, and came down into the plain of Argos. The Corinthians, Pellenians and Phliasians marched by another steep road. The Boeotians, Megarians and Sicyonians were told to come down by the Nemean road, where the Argives were posted. Their task was to attack the Argive rear with their cavalry if the enemy advanced into the plain against Agis and his troops. When these arrangements were complete, Agis invaded the plain and began to ravage Saminthus and other places.

On discovering this, the Argives came up from Nemea, since day had now broken. On the way they met the Phliasian and Corinthian troops. They killed a few of the Phliasians, and perhaps lost a few more of their own men to the Corinthians. Meanwhile the Boeotians, Megarians and Sicyonians advanced on Nemea as instructed, and found the Argives gone. The Argives had come down on seeing their property ravaged, and were now forming for battle, with the Lacedaemonians doing the same. The Argives were now completely surrounded. The Lacedaemonians and their allies in the plain cut them off from their city. Above them stood the Corinthians, Phliasians and Pellenians, and on the Nemea side the Boeotians, Sicyonians and Megarians. They had no cavalry, since the Athenians alone among the allies had not yet come. Most of the Argives and their allies did not see how dangerous their position was. They thought they could not ask for a better field of battle, since they had cut off the Lacedaemonians in their own country and close to the city. But two men in the Argive army, Thrasylus, one of the five generals, and Alciphron, the Lacedaemonian proxenus, went to parley with Agis just as the armies were about to engage. They urged him not to bring on a battle. The Argives, they said, were ready to submit to fair and equal arbitration any complaints the Lacedaemonians might have against them, and to make a treaty and live at peace in future.

The Argives who said this spoke on their own authority, not by order of the people. Agis accepted their proposals, and did so without consulting the majority; he simply told one man, a high officer who accompanied the expedition. He granted the Argives a four months’ truce in which to fulfill their promises, and at once led the army off, giving no explanation to any of the other allies. Out of respect for the law, the Lacedaemonians and allies followed their general. But among themselves they blamed Agis loudly. He had left so fair a field, with the enemy hemmed in on every side by infantry and cavalry, and had done nothing worthy of their strength. This was in fact by far the finest Hellenic army ever brought together, and one had to see it while it was still united at Nemea. There were the Lacedaemonians in full force, and the Arcadians, Boeotians, Corinthians, Sicyonians, Pellenians, Phliasians and Megarians, each the flower of its own population. They thought themselves a match not merely for the Argive confederacy but for another one added to it. So the army withdrew, blaming Agis, and each man went home. The Argives, however, blamed even more loudly the men who had concluded the truce without consulting the people. They believed they had let an opportunity slip away with the Lacedaemonians such as they would never see again, since the fight would have taken place beneath the walls of their city and beside many brave allies. When they returned, therefore, they began to stone Thrasylus in the bed of the Charadrus, where they try all military cases before entering the city. Thrasylus took refuge at the altar and saved his life, but they confiscated his property.

After this a thousand Athenian heavy infantry and three hundred horse arrived under Laches and Nicostratus. The Argives were still unwilling to break the truce with the Lacedaemonians, and begged them to leave. They refused to bring them before the people, to whom the Athenians had a message to deliver, until the Mantineans and Eleans, who were still at Argos, pressed them with entreaties. The Athenians then spoke through Alcibiades, their ambassador on the spot. He told the Argives and the allies that they had no right to make a truce at all without the consent of their fellow confederates, and that now the Athenians had arrived so opportunely, the war ought to go on. The allies were convinced by these arguments and marched at once on Orchomenos. Only the Argives stayed behind at first; they had consented like the others, but eventually joined them. All of them now sat down before Orchomenos, besieged it and made assaults. One of their reasons for wanting the place was that the Lacedaemonians had lodged hostages from Arcadia there. The Orchomenians feared the weakness of their wall and the size of the enemy force, and the danger of perishing before relief came. They capitulated on these terms: they would join the league, give hostages of their own to the Mantineans, and hand over the ones the Lacedaemonians had lodged with them. With Orchomenos secured, the allies consulted over which of the remaining places to attack next. The Eleans pressed for Lepreum and the Mantineans for Tegea. The Argives and Athenians backed the Mantineans, and the Eleans went home in a rage that their vote for Lepreum had been lost. The rest of the allies prepared at Mantinea to go against Tegea, where a party inside had arranged to hand the town over to them.

Meanwhile the Lacedaemonians had come back from Argos after concluding the four months’ truce. They bitterly blamed Agis for not having subdued Argos. They thought they had never had such an opportunity, since it was no easy matter to bring so many good allies together. When news came that Orchomenos had been captured, their anger grew still greater. Against all precedent, in the heat of the moment they came close to deciding to raze his house and to fine him ten thousand drachmae. Agis begged them to do none of this. He promised to make up for his fault by good service in the field, and said that if he failed, they could then do to him whatever they pleased. So they refrained from razing his house or fining him, as they had threatened. But they passed a law, which had never before existed at Lacedaemon, giving him ten Spartans as counsellors, without whose consent he would have no power to lead an army out of the city.

At this moment word came from their friends in Tegea: unless the Lacedaemonians appeared quickly, Tegea would go over to the Argives and their allies, if it had not already done so. On this news a force marched out from Lacedaemon, made up of the Spartans and Helots and all their people, immediately and on a scale never seen before. They advanced to Orestheum in Maenalia. There they told the Arcadians in their league to follow close behind them to Tegea. They themselves went on as far as Orestheum, and from there sent back the sixth part of the Spartans, the oldest and the youngest men, to guard their homes. With the rest of their army they reached Tegea, and their Arcadian allies soon joined them. At the same time they sent word to Corinth, to the Boeotians, the Phocians and the Locrians, with orders to come as quickly as possible to Mantinea. These allies had little notice. The enemy’s country lay right across their line of communication and blocked it, so it was not easy to get through except all together, waiting for one another. Nevertheless they made what haste they could. Meanwhile the Lacedaemonians and the Arcadian allies who had joined them entered the territory of Mantinea. They encamped near the temple of Heracles and began to plunder the country.

The Argives and their allies saw them there, and at once took up a strong and difficult position and formed in battle order. The Lacedaemonians immediately advanced against them and came within a stone’s throw or a javelin’s cast. Then one of the older men saw how strong the enemy’s position was, and called out to Agis that he meant to cure one evil with another. He meant that Agis, by this untimely haste, wished to make amends for his retreat from Argos, which had been so much blamed. Agis then quickly led his army back without engaging, either because of this call or because of a sudden idea of his own. He entered the Tegean territory and began to divert into Mantinean land the water over which the Mantineans and Tegeans are always fighting, because of the great damage it does to whichever country it flows into. His aim was to bring the Argives and their allies down from the hill to resist the diversion of the water, as they were sure to do once they knew of it, and so to fight the battle in the plain. He therefore stayed where he was that day, busy diverting the water. The Argives and their allies were at first astonished that the enemy had retreated so suddenly after coming so near, and did not know what to make of it. But when he had gone and vanished without any move by them to pursue, they began to find fault with their generals again. These generals had already let the Lacedaemonians get away when they were so happily cut off before Argos, and now again allowed them to run off with no one pursuing. The Lacedaemonians were escaping at their ease, the Argives complained, while the Argive army was being betrayed at its ease. The generals, half-stunned for the moment, afterwards led the army down from the hill and went forward and encamped in the plain, intending to attack the enemy.

The next day the Argives and their allies drew up in the order in which they meant to fight if they happened to meet the enemy. The Lacedaemonians were coming back from the water to their old camp by the temple of Heracles. Suddenly they saw their adversaries right in front of them, all in perfect order and advanced from the hill. The Lacedaemonians do not remember ever having experienced a shock like this one. There was hardly any time to prepare. They fell into their ranks at once and in haste, with Agis, their king, directing everything as the law requires. When a king is in the field, every command comes from him. He gives the word to the Polemarchs, they pass it to the Lochages, these to the Pentecostyes, these again to the Enomotarchs, and these last to the Enomoties. All orders needed go the same way and quickly reach the troops. Almost the whole Lacedaemonian army, except for a small part, consists of officers under officers, so the responsibility for what is to be done falls on many.

In this battle the Sciritae held the left wing of the Lacedaemonian army, a post that they always have to themselves alone in a Lacedaemonian army. Next to them stood the soldiers of Brasidas from Thrace, with the Neodamodes beside them. Then came the Lacedaemonians themselves, company after company, with the Arcadians of Heraea at their side. After these were the Maenalians, and on the right wing the Tegeans, with a few Lacedaemonians at the far end. Their cavalry was posted on the two wings. That was the Lacedaemonian formation. Their opponents were drawn up as follows. On the right were the Mantineans, since the action was taking place in their country. Next to them were the allies from Arcadia. After these came the thousand picked men of the Argives, whom the state had trained in arms for a long time at public expense. Next to them stood the rest of the Argives, then their allies the Cleonaeans and Orneans, and last, on the extreme left, the Athenians, with their own cavalry beside them.

These were the order and the forces of the two sides. The Lacedaemonian army looked the larger. But I could not state with any accuracy the numbers of either army, or of the contingents that made them up. The Lacedaemonian government is secretive, so their numbers were not known. And men are so inclined to boast about the forces of their own country that the estimates given of the Lacedaemonians were not trusted. Still, the following calculation makes it possible to estimate the numbers of the Lacedaemonians present on this occasion. There were seven companies in the field, not counting the Sciritae, who numbered six hundred men. Each company had four Pentecostyes, and each Pentecosty four Enomoties. The first rank of an Enomoty consisted of four soldiers. As to the depth, the men had not all been drawn up alike but as each captain chose, though they were generally ranged eight deep. The first rank along the whole line, not counting the Sciritae, consisted of four hundred and forty-eight men.

With the armies now on the eve of engaging, each contingent received some words of encouragement from its own commander. The Mantineans were reminded that they were fighting for their country, and that they would be avoiding a return to servitude after having known empire. The Argives were told that they would be contending for their ancient supremacy, to regain their once equal share of Peloponnese, of which they had so long been deprived, and to punish an enemy and a neighbor for a thousand wrongs. The Athenians were reminded of the glory of winning the honors of the day with so many brave allies in arms. They were told that a victory over the Lacedaemonians in Peloponnese would cement and extend their empire, and would also keep Attica safe from invasion in future. Such were the appeals addressed to the Argives and their allies. The Lacedaemonians, meanwhile, exhorted one another man to man, with war-songs in the ranks, each to remember as a brave comrade what he had learnt before. They were well aware that long training in action was worth more for their safety than any brief spoken exhortation, however well delivered.

After this they joined battle. The Argives and their allies advanced with haste and fury, the Lacedaemonians slowly and to the music of many flute-players. This is a standing institution in their army and has nothing to do with religion. Its purpose is to make them advance evenly, stepping in time, without breaking their order, as large armies are apt to do at the moment of engaging.

Just before the battle was joined, King Agis resolved on the following maneuver. All armies behave alike in this: on going into action they are forced out somewhat toward their right wing, and each overlaps its adversary’s left with its own right. This happens because fear makes every man do his best to shelter his unarmed side behind the shield of the man next to him on the right, thinking that the more closely the shields are locked together, the better he will be protected. The man chiefly responsible is the first on the right wing, who is always trying to keep his unarmed side away from the enemy, and the same apprehension makes the rest follow him. On this occasion the Mantineans reached with their wing far beyond the Sciritae, and the Lacedaemonians and Tegeans reached still farther beyond the Athenians, because their army was the largest. Agis was afraid that his left would be surrounded, and thought that the Mantineans outflanked it too far. He therefore ordered the Sciritae and the Brasideans to move out of their place in the ranks and make the line even with the Mantineans. He also told the Polemarchs Hipponoidas and Aristocles to fill the gap thus formed by throwing themselves into it with two companies taken from the right wing. He thought that his right would still be strong enough and to spare, and that the line facing the Mantineans would gain in solidity.

However, he gave these orders at the moment of the onset and at short notice, and it so happened that Aristocles and Hipponoidas would not move over. For this offense they were afterwards banished from Sparta, as guilty of cowardice. Meanwhile the enemy closed in before the Sciritae had time to fill the breach in question. (Agis, seeing that the two companies had not moved over, had ordered the Sciritae to return to their place.) It was now that the Lacedaemonians, utterly worsted in skill, showed themselves superior in courage. As soon as they came to close quarters with the enemy, the Mantinean right broke the Sciritae and Brasideans. Bursting into the unclosed breach in the line with their allies and the thousand picked Argives, they cut up and surrounded the Lacedaemonians and drove them in full rout to the wagons, slaying some of the older men on guard there. But the Lacedaemonians, though worsted in this part of the field, were successful with the rest of their army, especially in the center, where the three hundred knights, as they are called, fought around King Agis. They fell on the older men of the Argives, and the five companies so named, and on the Cleonaeans, the Orneans and the Athenians next to them, and routed them instantly. Most of these did not even wait to strike a blow but gave way the moment the Lacedaemonians came on, and some were even trodden underfoot, in their fear of being overtaken by their assailants.

The army of the Argives and their allies, having given way in this quarter, was now completely cut in two. At the same time the Lacedaemonian and Tegean right closed round the Athenians with the troops that outflanked them, so that the Athenians were caught between two fires, surrounded on one side and already defeated on the other. Indeed they would have suffered more severely than any other part of the army, had it not been for the cavalry they had with them. Agis also saw the distress of his left, which was opposed to the Mantineans and the thousand Argives, and ordered the whole army to advance to the support of the defeated wing. While this was going on, the enemy moved past and slanted away from them, and the Athenians escaped at their leisure, together with the beaten Argive division. Meanwhile the Mantineans, their allies and the picked body of the Argives stopped pressing the enemy. They saw their friends defeated and the Lacedaemonians advancing on them in full force, and they took to flight. Many of the Mantineans perished, but the bulk of the picked body of the Argives made good their escape. The flight and retreat, however, were neither hurried nor long. The Lacedaemonians fought long and stubbornly until their enemy was routed, but once that was achieved, they pursued only for a short time and not far.

Such was the battle, as nearly as possible as I have described it. It was the greatest that had occurred among the Hellenes for a very long time, and it was fought by the most considerable states. The Lacedaemonians took up a position in front of the enemy’s dead and immediately set up a trophy and stripped the slain. They collected their own dead and carried them back to Tegea, where they buried them, and they returned those of the enemy under truce. The Argives, Orneans and Cleonaeans had seven hundred killed, the Mantineans two hundred, and the Athenians and Aeginetans also two hundred, together with both their generals. On the Lacedaemonian side, the allies suffered no loss worth speaking of. As for the Lacedaemonians themselves, it was difficult to learn the truth, but it is said that about three hundred of them were slain.

While the battle was impending, Pleistoanax, the other king, set out with a reinforcement made up of the oldest and youngest men. He got as far as Tegea, where he heard of the victory, and went back again. The Lacedaemonians also sent word and turned back the allies from Corinth and from beyond the Isthmus. They then returned home themselves, dismissed their allies, and kept the Carnean holidays, which happened to fall at that time. The charges that the Hellenes had brought against them at the time were all wiped out by this single action. They had been accused of cowardice because of the disaster on the island, and generally of mismanagement and slowness. It was now thought that fortune might have humbled them, but that the men themselves were the same as ever.

On the day before this battle, the Epidaurians invaded the deserted Argive territory with all their forces and cut off many of the guards left there in the absence of the Argive army. After the battle, three thousand Elean heavy infantry arrived to aid the Mantineans, together with a reinforcement of one thousand Athenians. All these allies marched at once against Epidaurus, while the Lacedaemonians were keeping the Carnea. They divided the work among them and began to build a wall round the city. The rest left off, but the Athenians at once finished the part assigned to them round Cape Heraeum. All the allies joined in leaving a garrison in the fortification, and then returned to their respective cities.

Summer now came to an end. In the first days of the next winter, when the Carnean holidays were over, the Lacedaemonians took the field. They arrived at Tegea and sent on to Argos proposals of accommodation. They had long had a party in the town that wished to overthrow the democracy, and after the battle that had been fought, this party was far better placed to persuade the people to listen to terms. Their plan was first to make a treaty with the Lacedaemonians, to be followed by an alliance, and after this to fall upon the commons. Lichas, son of Arcesilaus, the Argive proxenus, accordingly arrived at Argos with two proposals from Lacedaemon, one to regulate the conditions of war and the other of peace, according to which the Argives preferred. After much discussion, with Alcibiades happening to be in the town, the Lacedaemonian party, which now ventured to act openly, persuaded the Argives to accept the proposal for accommodation. It ran as follows:
The assembly of the Lacedaemonians agrees to treat with the Argives on the following terms:
1. The Argives shall give back to the Orchomenians their children and to the Maenalians their men, and shall give back to the Lacedaemonians the men they hold in Mantinea.

2. They shall evacuate Epidaurus and raze the fortification there. If the Athenians refuse to withdraw from Epidaurus, they shall be declared enemies of the Argives and of the Lacedaemonians, and of the allies of the Lacedaemonians and the allies of the Argives.
3. If the Lacedaemonians have any children in their custody, they shall return every one of them to his city.
4. As to the offering to the god, the Argives, if they wish, shall impose an oath on the Epidaurians; if not, they shall swear it themselves.
5. All the cities in Peloponnese, small and great alike, shall be independent and keep their ancestral customs.

6. If any of the powers outside Peloponnese invades Peloponnesian territory, the contracting parties shall unite to repel them, on such terms as they may agree upon as being most fair for the Peloponnesians.

7. All allies of the Lacedaemonians outside Peloponnese shall be on the same footing as the Lacedaemonians, and the allies of the Argives shall be on the same footing as the Argives, and shall be left in enjoyment of their own possessions.
8. This treaty shall be shown to the allies and shall be concluded if they approve. If the allies think fit, they may send the treaty home to be considered there.

The Argives began by accepting this proposal, and the Lacedaemonian army returned home from Tegea. After this, dealings between the two cities were renewed. Not long afterwards the same party arranged for the Argives to give up the league with the Mantineans, Eleans and Athenians, and to make a treaty and alliance with the Lacedaemonians. This was accordingly done, on the following terms:
The Lacedaemonians and Argives agree to a treaty and alliance for fifty years on the following terms:
1. All disputes shall be decided by fair and impartial arbitration, in accordance with the customs of the two countries.

2. The rest of the cities in Peloponnese may be included in this treaty and alliance as independent and sovereign, in full enjoyment of what they possess, all disputes being decided by fair and impartial arbitration, in accordance with the customs of those cities.

3. All allies of the Lacedaemonians outside Peloponnese shall be on the same footing as the Lacedaemonians themselves, and the allies of the Argives shall be on the same footing as the Argives themselves, continuing to enjoy what they possess.
4. If it shall anywhere be necessary to make an expedition in common, the Lacedaemonians and Argives shall consult on it and decide, as may be most fair for the allies.

5. If any of the cities, whether inside or outside Peloponnese, has a question of frontiers or any other matter, it must be settled. But if one allied city has a quarrel with another allied city, it must be referred to some third city that both parties think impartial. Private citizens shall have their disputes decided according to the laws of their several countries.

When the treaty and the above alliance were concluded, each party at once released everything held, whether acquired by war or otherwise. From then on they acted in common, and voted to receive neither herald nor embassy from the Athenians unless the Athenians evacuated their forts and withdrew from Peloponnese, and also to make neither peace nor war with anyone except jointly. They did not lack zeal. Both parties sent envoys to the Thracian places and to Perdiccas, and persuaded him to join their league. He did not break off from Athens at once, although he was minded to do so on seeing the way shown him by Argos, the original home of his family. They also renewed their old oaths with the Chalcidians and took new ones. The Argives, besides, sent ambassadors to the Athenians, bidding them evacuate the fort at Epidaurus. The Athenians saw that their own men were outnumbered by the rest of the garrison, and sent Demosthenes to bring them out. On his arrival this general arranged a gymnastic contest as a pretext, got the rest of the garrison out of the place, and shut the gates behind them. Afterwards the Athenians renewed their treaty with the Epidaurians and by their own act gave up the fortress.

After the defection of Argos from the league, the Mantineans held out at first, but in the end they found themselves powerless without the Argives, and they too came to terms with Lacedaemon and gave up their sovereignty over the towns. The Lacedaemonians and Argives, each a thousand strong, now took the field together. The Lacedaemonians first went by themselves to Sicyon and made the government there more oligarchical than before. Then both armies united and put down the democracy at Argos and set up an oligarchy favorable to Lacedaemon. These events occurred at the close of the winter, just before spring, and the fourteenth year of the war ended. The next summer the people of Dium, in Athos, revolted from the Athenians to the Chalcidians, and the Lacedaemonians settled affairs in Achaea in a way more agreeable to the interests of their country. Meanwhile the popular party at Argos little by little gathered new strength and courage. They waited for the time of the Gymnopaedic festival at Lacedaemon and then fell upon the oligarchs. After a fight in the city, victory went to the commons, who slew some of their opponents and banished others. For a long while the Lacedaemonians took no action on the messages of their friends at Argos. At last they put off the Gymnopaediae and marched to their aid. But at Tegea they learned that the oligarchs had been defeated, and they refused to go any further in spite of the entreaties of those who had escaped. They returned home and kept the festival. Later, envoys arrived with messages from the Argives in the town and from the exiles, when the allies were also at Sparta. After much had been said on both sides, the Lacedaemonians decided that the party in the town had done wrong and resolved to march against Argos, but they kept delaying and putting the matter off. Meanwhile the commons at Argos, in fear of the Lacedaemonians, began again to court the Athenian alliance, which they were convinced would be of the greatest service to them. They accordingly proceeded to build long walls to the sea, so that if they were blockaded by land, they could, with the help of the Athenians, have the advantage of importing what they wanted by sea. Some of the cities in Peloponnese were also privy to the building of these walls. The Argives with all their people, women and slaves not excepted, addressed themselves to the work, and carpenters and masons came to them from Athens.

Summer was now over. The following winter the Lacedaemonians heard of the walls that were being built and marched against Argos with their allies, except the Corinthians. They also had contacts inside the city itself. Agis, son of Archidamus, their king, was in command. The support they counted on within the town came to nothing. They did, however, take and raze the walls that were being built. They also captured the Argive town of Hysiae and killed all the freemen who fell into their hands, and then went back and dispersed, every man to his city. After this the Argives marched into Phlius and plundered it for harboring their exiles, most of whom had settled there, and then returned home. The same winter the Athenians blockaded Macedonia, on account of the league Perdiccas had entered into with the Argives and Lacedaemonians, and also of his breach of his engagements on the occasion of the expedition prepared by Athens against the Chalcidians in the direction of Thrace and against Amphipolis, under the command of Nicias, son of Niceratus. That expedition had to be broken up mainly because of his desertion. He was therefore proclaimed an enemy. And thus the winter ended, and the fifteenth year of the war ended with it.
